h: Priest holes, a bloodstain and a walk along the canal
p: Baddesley Clinton's most gripping story comes from 1591, when the house was a secret refuge for Catholic priests at a time when practising their faith was dangerous. During a raid, several Jesuit priests hid from searchers in a hiding place built into the old drains beneath the house, and they escaped undetected. You can see the priest holes today, and kids are usually fascinated by just how cramped they are.

There is a darker legend too. A stain on the library floor is said to be the blood of a priest killed by Nicholas Brome, a former owner, in the 15th century. Whether it is real or not, it is a cracking story to tell in a hushed voice.

Allow around three hours to see the house, gardens and lakeside. If you have time, add Packwood House, a few miles away. Its famous yew garden, with clipped trees said to represent the Sermon on the Mount, is a real one-off.

For something different, the Hatton Locks on the Grand Union Canal are nearby. This flight of 21 locks climbs the hill towards Warwick and is a lovely place for a towpath walk, watching narrowboats work their way up. Kenilworth Castle and Warwick Castle are also both within easy driving distance if you want to make a weekend of exploring Warwickshire.
